For example, an incorrect signal at point B could be caused by a number of faults.
Incorrect Vcc, a malfunctioning amplifier, or a malfunctioning feedback circuit can all cause the signal at point B to be incorrect.
Usually, an interruption anywhere in the oscillator results in no output.
Since many different faults could cause the same symptoms, a basic troubleshooting method is needed.
Once you have measured the output of the circuit and determined it to be incorrect, measure Vcc to ensure correct supply voltage.
If Vcc checks good, the next stage to suspect trouble is in the amplifier since it contains a semiconductor.
To check the transistor in the amplifier, disconnect Vcc and perform continuity checks with an ohmmeter or use a digital meter's diode junction test.............

The same test holds true for the Base-to-Collector junction. Remember, resistance is high one way, or no current flow.
And a low resistance or current flow is the other way. The actual polarity or direction is not important. The fact that you get a distinct different reading with the leads reversed is the key.
If the transistor in the amplifier checks good, the next stage to check is the feedback circuit.
Resistance measurements indicate much about the condition of the feedback circuit.
For example, anytime you measure zero ohms or infinite ohms across the resonant circuit, it is faulted.
Measuring across each component determines open or shorted inductors and shorted capacitors.
Open capacitors can only be detected by testing with an RCL bridge or replacing the capacitor and rechecking the output.
Correct resistance measurements should be low and reflect the DC resistance of the inductors. The capacitors measure infinite DC resistance.
